experiences.description: Grading around 300 assignments per term and giving students feedback on data structures and complexity analysis.
highlights: Graded roughly 300 assignments per term across multiple programming languages
Evaluated correctness, algorithmic efficiency, and code quality
Gave detailed feedback on trees, graphs, hash maps, and complexity analysis
experiences.intro:
The role

I work as a teaching assistant for Data Structures and Algorithms at Acadia University, supporting students through the course that most of the computer science program is built on top of.

Each term I grade around 300 assignments written in several different programming languages. Every submission gets read for three things: whether it is correct, whether the approach is efficient, and whether the code is something another person could maintain.
experiences.body:
Feedback over marks

Most of the work is written feedback rather than the mark itself. Students submit implementations of trees, graphs, and hash maps, and the interesting part is usually the gap between a solution that passes the tests and a solution that scales. I point out where a nested loop hides a quadratic cost, or where a different structure would remove the problem entirely.

What it changed about how I code

Reading that many implementations of the same problem makes patterns obvious very quickly. It also made me far stricter about naming and structure in my own projects, because I now know exactly how it feels to read code that was written in a hurry.

experiences.intro:
The role

I work the IT Service Desk at Acadia University, handling tickets and walk-ins from students and faculty. The problems range from malware and network failures to Microsoft account access that has to be fixed before someone can teach a class.
experiences.body:
Debugging with a person in front of you

Service desk work is debugging under a constraint you do not get in a codebase: the person affected is standing there. You have to reproduce the issue, narrow it down, and explain what happened without jargon, often in a few minutes.

Why it matters for backend work

Support work is where you see how systems fail in practice rather than in theory. It is a steady reminder that authentication, permissions, and error messages are not edge cases in a spec, they are the parts people actually collide with.

experiences.intro:
The role

I joined Wayfair through Extern as an AI Agent Engineering Extern and finished the program with Top Performer recognition.

The work was building agent pipelines rather than one-off prompts: five production pipelines in n8n, running on Docker, wired to Google Gemini and HuggingFace models.
experiences.body:
Pipelines, not prompts

A model call is the easy part. The real work was everything around it: triggering the run, shaping the input, validating what came back, and handling the cases where the model returned something unusable. Running the pipelines in Docker kept the environment reproducible instead of only working on one machine.

What I took from it

Working across five pipelines rather than one showed me how much of AI engineering is ordinary backend engineering. Retries, structured output, and clear boundaries between steps mattered far more than clever prompting.

posts.title: Five Agent Pipelines in n8n
posts.cardSummary: What building AI agents in production taught me about ordinary backend engineering.
posts.summary: Notes from the Wayfair externship: why the model call was the least interesting part of each pipeline.
posts.content:
The model call is the easy part

During my externship with Wayfair through Extern I built five production AI agent pipelines in n8n, running on Docker, using Google Gemini and HuggingFace models. Going in, I assumed the hard part would be the prompting. It was not.

Every pipeline spent most of its complexity on the same unglamorous things: what triggers a run, how the input is shaped before it reaches the model, how the response is validated, and what happens when the model returns something unusable.

Structured output or nothing

An agent that returns prose is a demo. An agent that returns predictable JSON is something you can put downstream of other systems. Forcing a schema on the output, then failing loudly when it did not match, made the pipelines far easier to reason about.

Docker kept it honest

Running the pipelines in Docker meant the environment was the same every time. That sounds obvious, but it is the difference between a workflow that runs on one laptop and one that a team can actually operate.

What I would tell myself at the start

Treat agent work as backend work. Retries, timeouts, validation, and clear boundaries between steps matter more than clever prompt wording.

posts.title: What Grading 300 Assignments Taught Me
posts.cardSummary: Reading the same algorithm 300 different ways changes how you write your own code.
posts.summary: Lessons from teaching data structures and algorithms at Acadia University.
posts.content:
Three hundred versions of one problem

As a teaching assistant for Data Structures and Algorithms I grade around 300 assignments a term, across several languages. Every submission is read for correctness, algorithmic efficiency, and code quality.

Patterns show up fast

When you read that many implementations of trees, graphs, and hash maps, the common failure modes stop being theoretical. The same nested loop hiding a quadratic cost appears again and again, usually in code that passes every test.

The mark is not the point

Most of my time goes into written feedback rather than the number at the top. Pointing out where a different structure removes the problem entirely is worth more than a deduction.

It made me a stricter reader of my own code

After a term of grading, I am far more careful about naming and structure in my own projects. I know exactly how it feels to read something written in a hurry.

posts.title: Turning Spreadsheets Into Answers
posts.cardSummary: Businalyst started as a spreadsheet problem, not a Django problem.
posts.summary: How working backwards from the user's question shaped the API behind Businalyst.
posts.content:
Start from the question

Businalyst is a full-stack analytics app built with Django and React (Vite) that helps small and mid-sized businesses turn Excel and CSV exports into something they can act on. The interesting constraint was never the framework, it was that the people using it already had their data and still could not answer basic questions about it.

Designing the API backwards

I built the REST API by working backwards from those questions rather than forwards from the database schema. Upload, parse, summarise, explain. Pandas and NumPy handle the middle, and the endpoints stay shaped like the workflow instead of the tables.

Shipping it

I managed the deployment end to end onto a custom domain, and the team worked through Git and GitHub. Getting it live early surfaced the messy file formats far faster than any amount of local testing would have.
